topics.covers: Immediate danger, the 24-hour helpline, protection orders
topics.sum: If you or your children are in danger, call 999. If you can’t speak, stay on the line and press 55 when asked. The helplines below are free and confidential, and can help you plan to leave safely.

gov.t: Domestic abuse: how to get help
Get an injunction if you’ve been the victim of domestic abuse

links.d: Runs the National Domestic Abuse Helpline. Its website explains your options, including how to cover your tracks online.
Live chat, a survivors’ forum and a directory of local services.
Confidential help for men experiencing domestic abuse, by phone, webchat or email.

topics.advice: A family solicitor can apply for a protection order quickly. See Legal aid and court fees for help paying.

topics.covers: Who can apply, joint or sole, the online service, the waiting period
topics.sum: You can apply on your own or together, usually online. There are set waiting periods between the steps, and GOV.UK gives the current ones. Ending a civil partnership works in much the same way.

gov.t: Get a divorce
Apply for a divorce

links.d: Plain guides to divorce and separation, and local advisers you can talk to.

topics.advice: Citizens Advice, or a family solicitor if your situation is complicated.

topics.covers: Agreeing between you, parenting plans, when court is needed
topics.sum: Most parents agree arrangements between themselves, sometimes with a mediator’s help. Court is a last resort, and you’ll usually need to go to a mediation meeting first.

gov.t: Making child arrangements if you divorce or separate
Making child arrangements: mediation

links.d: Its parenting plan helps you agree arrangements and write them down.

topics.advice: A family mediator, or a family solicitor if you can’t agree.

topics.covers: What a MIAM is, the voucher, who it covers, finding a mediator
topics.sum: A MIAM is a first meeting with a mediator, which you usually need before you can apply to court. A government voucher scheme can pay towards mediation about children. GOV.UK has the current amount and when the scheme ends.

gov.t: Family Mediation Voucher Scheme
Money and property: get help agreeing

links.d: Find an accredited mediator near you, and check who can offer vouchers.

topics.advice: An accredited family mediator can tell you whether the voucher applies to you.

topics.covers: Who can get legal aid, help paying court fees, fee-free protection orders
topics.sum: Legal aid for family cases is limited, but it’s often available for mediation and where there’s been domestic abuse. On a low income, you may get help paying court fees.

gov.t: Legal aid
Legal aid: family mediation
Get help paying court and tribunal fees

links.d: Check whether you can get legal aid, and find a legal aid adviser.

topics.advice: Civil Legal Advice can tell you whether you qualify.

topics.covers: Reporting the change, a couple claim becoming single claims, Housing Benefit
topics.sum: Tell the offices that pay your benefits as soon as you separate. A joint Universal Credit claim ends, and you each make your own claim.

gov.t: Report a change in your circumstances
Universal Credit: further information for couples

links.d: A free calculator for what you could get on your own.

topics.advice: Citizens Advice can go through your claim with you.

topics.covers: The single person discount, telling your council
topics.sum: If you now live on your own, you may get a discount on your Council Tax. You apply to your own council.

gov.t: Council Tax

links.d: Your council’s own page explains its discounts and how to apply.

topics.covers: Who claims, a child living with the other parent, the High Income Child Benefit Charge
topics.sum: Only one person can get Child Benefit for a child, usually the parent they mainly live with. If that changes, the claim needs to change too. Separating can also change whether the High Income Child Benefit Charge applies to you.

gov.t: Child Benefit if your child lives with someone else
High Income Child Benefit Charge: if your circumstances change

topics.advice: The Child Benefit Office, or Citizens Advice.

topics.covers: Family-based arrangements, the Child Maintenance Service, how it’s worked out
topics.sum: You can agree child maintenance between you, or use the Child Maintenance Service if you can’t. Its way of working it out is a useful guide either way.

gov.t: Make a private child maintenance arrangement
How we work out child maintenance

topics.advice: Citizens Advice, or a family solicitor.

topics.covers: Reaching an agreement, making it binding, financial disclosure
topics.sum: You can agree how to split money, property and pensions yourselves. To make it legally binding, you ask the court to turn it into a consent order. Either way, you each need to show the other everything you have: that’s financial disclosure, in the next section.

gov.t: Money and property when you divorce or separate

links.d: Step-by-step guides to sorting out money when you separate.
Family solicitors and mediators who work to a code of practice.

topics.advice: A family solicitor can check an agreement before it goes to the court.

topics.covers: Capital Gains Tax on transfers between you, Marriage Allowance
topics.sum: Moving things between you can affect Capital Gains Tax, and the rules depend on when you separated. If one of you transferred Marriage Allowance to the other, it can be cancelled.

gov.t: Tax when you transfer assets
Capital Gains Tax: separation and divorce

topics.advice: An accountant or tax adviser, if you’re moving property, shares or a business between you.

topics.sum: Pensions are often among the largest things to share. You can split one with a pension sharing order, or offset its value against other things. Either way, start by asking each provider for a valuation.

links.d: Free, government-backed guidance on pensions when you divorce or separate.

topics.advice: For larger or more complicated pensions, ask your solicitor or mediator about a pensions expert.

topics.covers: Staying, moving out, help if you could become homeless
topics.sum: Before anyone moves out, find out what rights you each have to stay in the home. If you might become homeless, your council has to help, and the sooner you contact it the better.

links.d: Housing advice, including a helpline and webchat.
For help if you might become homeless.

topics.advice: Shelter, or a family solicitor about your rights to the home.

topics.covers: Someone to talk to, support for children
topics.sum: Separating is hard. Talking to someone helps, whether that’s a friend, your GP or a helpline. Children cope better when they know what’s happening, and that it isn’t their fault.

links.d: Someone to talk to, any time, by phone, email or letter.
Information and support for your mental health.
For children and young people: free and confidential.

disclosure.covers: What each of you must show the other and the court, and the forms for it
disclosure.sum: Before the court will approve how you split things, it needs to see what you both have. How much you show, and on which form, depends on whether you’ve agreed.

routes.when: You agree how to split things
routes.d: You write up what you’ve agreed as a draft consent order and send it to the court with a D81, which summarises what you each have so a judge can check it’s fair. Some applications need Form A too. You can apply once the conditional order is made, and the order takes effect after the final order.

You apply with Form A. You each then fill in Form E, a full financial statement with documents, and exchange them. The court then takes you through its steps to a decision, and you can still settle along the way.
Other forms exist for other kinds of application, such as changing an order you already have. GOV.UK lists them.

forms.A: Notice of intention to proceed with a financial application

checklist: Recent statements for every bank, savings and investment account
A valuation from each pension provider
Your home: a valuation and the latest mortgage statement
Your income: payslips and your P60, or accounts if you’re self-employed
What you owe: loans, credit cards and finance agreements
Anything else of value: cars, policies, shares, a business
